text:
In the year that the commander in chief came to Ashdod, sent by Sargon king of Assyria, he fought against Ashdod and captured it.[^1]

[^1]: "Commander in chief" renders an Assyrian military title (Tartan), the second-in-command of the army.

versions.text: In the year that the commander in chief came to Ashdod, sent by Sargon king of Assyria, he fought against Ashdod and captured it.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew term is a borrowed Assyrian military title rather than a personal name; a brief footnote helps hearers and readers understand why a title, not a name, appears here. No change to the verse text itself is needed.

text: At that time the LORD spoke through Isaiah son of Amoz: "Go, take off the sackcloth from your waist and remove the sandals from your feet." And he did so, going stripped and barefoot.

versions.text: At that time the LORD spoke through Isaiah son of Amoz: "Go, strip the sackcloth from your waist and take the sandals off your feet." And he did so, going stripped and barefoot.
versions.explanation: The verb פִתַּחְתָּ means to loosen or untie a garment, and using "strip" here immediately before "going stripped" creates an awkward echo when read aloud. Varying the verbs keeps the rhythm clean and stays close to the Hebrew.

text: Then the LORD said, "Just as my servant Isaiah has gone stripped and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush,
so the king of Assyria will lead away the captives of Egypt and the exiles of Cush, young and old alike, stripped and barefoot, with buttocks bared—the shame of Egypt.
Then they will be dismayed and put to shame because of Cush, their hope, and Egypt, their boast.
And in that day the inhabitants of this coastland will say, "Look what has become of our hope, the one we fled to for help and rescue from the king of Assyria! How then can we escape?"
